To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the market allocation of resources in an economy with oligopolistic firms and endogenous innovation is not efficient and that, in equilibrium, firm size is determined by the number of firms and by the extent of the market.

(i) in the long run, the number of oligopolists is endogenous and depends on the rate of growth of the economy; (ii) the market allocation of resources in the presence of knowledge spillovers is not Pareto efficient; (iii) the market equilibrium is characterized by a trade-off between the number and the size of the firms.
the number of firms, the extent of the market, is determined endogenously by the zero-profit constraint.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the implications of the endogenous nature of the number of firms for the dynamics of innovation, the extent of the market and the efficiency of the market mechanism.
the implications of endogenous technological change for the structure of markets and the efficiency of resource allocation.

the following issues: the role of firm size and the number of firms in determining market concentration, the rate of innovation and the rate of growth; the determinants of the extent of the market and of its growth; and the nature of the distortion of the market allocation of resources.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is consistent with the empirical evidence and that it provides a coherent framework for analyzing the determinants of growth.
the number of firms is a determinant of the growth rate and that the market is a determinant of technological change.
, in this economy, the number of competing firms is determined by the zero-profit rule and is not an exogenous parameter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the market allocation is efficient in the sense that it maximizes the rate of technological change.
the number of firms in a competitive market is not determined by the size of the market but by the extent of the market.

we show that the extent of the market and the number of firms are determined endogenously in an economy where firms build their market positions by accumulating knowledge protected through secrecy, patents, and other appropriation devices.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in an economy where firms build their position by appropriating knowledge, the number of competing firms is endogenous and jointly determined with the rate of innovation by the zero-profit conditions.
firm size and rivalry are key determinants of the rate of innovation and growth.
the number of firms and their size are important determinants of growth.
